companyCaseStudy.title: How Cloudflare Absorbed a 17.2M RPS DDoS: Anycast, Edge Scrubbing, and Per-POP Load Sharing
companyCaseStudy.summary: In a now‑famous incident Cloudflare mitigated an HTTP DDoS that peaked at 17.2 million requests per second. The secret: an Anycasted global network (200+ POPs), pushing filtering and caching to the edge so the origin never saw the storm.
companyCaseStudy.explanation:
## Hook

A single customer was targeted with an application‑layer DDoS that peaked at 17.2 million HTTP requests per second. Left unprotected an origin and its load balancers would have been saturated in seconds. Cloudflare's distributed edge turned what could be a catastrophic outage into a contained incident.

---

## Problem

- Attack type: Layer 7 HTTP flood (high request RPS with legitimate-looking requests) 
- Peak: 17.2M requests/sec
- Risks: saturate TCP connection tables, overload web servers and app layers, exhaust autoscaling budgets, and cause customer downtime and huge cost spikes.

## Why this is hard (the challenges)

- Stateful defenses at origin (connection tracking, TCP stacks) are expensive at huge RPS.
- Distinguishing legitimate from malicious requests can be difficult; naive blocking risks false positives.
- Centralized scrubbing becomes a single point of failure; you need to spread the load.

Think of it like trying to stop a flood by putting a single sandbag at the end of the river: it doesn’t scale. You need levees distributed down the whole river.

---

## Solution narrative — Architecture & tactics

Cloudflare's approach combined three architectural pillars:

1. Anycast global ingress to distribute raw request volume across hundreds of POPs.
2. Push mitigation logic to the edge (WAF, rate‑limit, bot management, challenge/captcha) so filtering happens as close to the attacker as possible.
3. Cache aggressively at edge to reduce origin trips and enable early‑drop decisions.

The distributed nature is critical: 17.2M RPS split across ~200 POPs is roughly 86k RPS per POP (17,200,000 / 200 = 86,000). That per‑POP number is manageable with efficient, stateless early‑drop rules.

### Key building blocks used

- Anycast IPs: single IP announced from 200+ points of presence so traffic is load‑balanced by BGP.
- Edge WAF & firewall rules: signature and behavioural blocks applied at the first hop.
- Rate limiting & connection throttling: per IP / per URI rules to cut obvious floods.
- Challenge / CAPTCHA flows for suspicious sessions to separate humans from bots.
- Global telemetry & auto‑tuning to create and test blocking rules in near‑real time.
- Cache + origin shielding to keep cache hit rate high and limit origin exposure.

---

## Architecture (mermaid)

```mermaid
graph LR
  Internet[Internet / Attackers]
  Internet -->|BGP Anycast| POP1[PoP 1]\n(Edge)
  Internet -->|BGP Anycast| POP2[PoP 2]\n(Edge)
  Internet -->|BGP Anycast| POPN[PoP N]\n(Edge)
  POP1 --> WAF1[WAF / Rate Limit / Bot Challenge]
  POP2 --> WAF2[WAF / Rate Limit / Bot Challenge]
  POPN --> WAFN[WAF / Rate Limit / Bot Challenge]
  WAF1 --> Cache1[Edge Cache]
  WAF2 --> Cache2[Edge Cache]
  WAFN --> CacheN[Edge Cache]
  Cache1 -->|Cache Miss| Origin[Customer Origin]
  Cache2 -->|Cache Miss| Origin
  CacheN -->|Cache Miss| Origin
  WAF1 --> Telemetry[Metrics & Auto‑Rules]
  WAF2 --> Telemetry
  WAFN --> Telemetry
```

(Each PoP does early filtering; only allowed or cache‑miss traffic is forwarded to origin.)

---

## Before vs After (conceptual)

| Metric | Without global edge protection | With Cloudflare edge scrubbing |
|--------|---------------------------------|---------------------------------|
| Peak incoming RPS seen by origin | 17.2M (would saturate) | ~0 (edge absorbed or filtered) |
| Per‑PoP RPS load | N/A (centralized) | ~86k (17.2M / 200 POPs) |
| Origin requests/sec (cached content) | FULL storm | Only cache misses & verified traffic |
| Availability for customer | Likely outage | Customer stayed online |

---

## Results & impact

- The attack peaked at 17.2M RPS and was absorbed at the edge — the origin never saw the full storm.
- By distributing ingress and enforcing stateless early drops, the per‑POP load was reduced to an order of magnitude that could be handled with software rules and minimal state.
- Customers kept serving legitimate traffic while malicious traffic was challenged, rate‑limited, or dropped.

Remark: the 17.2M number underscores why distribution matters. A centralized scrubbing fabric would need to scale to that RPS; distributing to 200+ POPs makes the problem tractable.

---

## Tactics you can copy

- Use Anycast or multiple ingress points so an attack is spread across many points of presence.
- Push decision logic to the edge — early, stateless filters are cheap and fast.
- Cache aggressively to avoid origin trips; consider origin shielding to reduce duplicate requests.
- Automate telemetry -> rule generation (detect sudden spikes and create temporary rate‑limits or challenges).
- Adopt graduated responses: throttle -> challenge -> block, to minimize false positives.

---

## Short checklist for engineering teams

- Do we have multiple ingress points (Anycast, DNS + multi‑region LB)?
- Can we apply stateless, cheap rules at ingress? (rate limits, header checks)
- Is caching enabled for static resources and do we have an origin shield?
- Do we have automated telemetry + fast rule rollout?
keyTakeaways: Distribute ingress: 17.2M RPS / 200 POPs ≈ 86k RPS per POP — distribution makes massive floods manageable.
Push filtering to the edge (WAF, rate limits, challenges) so expensive stateful checks never hit origin.
Automate telemetry → temporary rules (throttle → challenge → block) to react in minutes without manual toil.

concept.title: Who Holds the Key? A Practical Guide to Distributed Locks
concept.summary: When multiple processes need exclusive access to a shared resource (cache rebuilds, leader work, serializing writes), *distributed locks* keep things correct and efficient. This guide explains how locks work across machines, practical patterns (Redis, ZooKeeper, DB), and pitfalls like deadlocks, clock skew, and single-point failures.
concept.explanation:
## WHY this matters

Imagine a busy workshop where multiple people reach for the same power drill. If two people try to use it at once bad things happen — safety problems, broken work, inconsistent results. In distributed systems the "drill" might be a cache entry being rebuilt, a migration step, or a payment processor. Without a reliable way to say "I have the drill", you'll get wasted work, race conditions, and subtle bugs.

Distributed locks let one participant *own* a resource at a time across the network. They are simple in concept but can be surprisingly tricky in practice.

---

## Analogy: The Tool Locker

- Local lock = a padlock on a single door: trivial inside one process.
- Distributed lock = a shared tool locker with an access card: every worker must swipe and hold the card for exclusive use.
- If the card reader breaks, everyone is blocked; if cards never expire, someone can hold it forever.

This analogy highlights the key realities: *mutual exclusion*, *lease/timeout*, and *failure modes*.

---

## How a simple distributed lock works (sequence)

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  WorkerA->>LockService: TRY_ACQUIRE(resource)
  LockService-->>WorkerA: OK(token)
  WorkerA->>Resource: do_work()
  WorkerA->>LockService: RELEASE(resource, token)
  LockService-->>WorkerA: OK
  WorkerB->>LockService: TRY_ACQUIRE(resource)
  LockService-->>WorkerB: OK(token2)
```

*WorkerA gets a token when it acquires the lock; it must present the same token when releasing to avoid unlocking someone else’s lock.*

---

## Common implementation approaches

| Approach | Pros | Cons | When to Use |
|---|---:|---|---|
| Redis SET NX with TTL | Fast, simple, low-latency | Single Redis instance = SPOF; careful with correct release | Short critical sections, simple coordination
| Redlock (multiple Redis masters) | More resilient than single Redis | Controversial guarantees under network partitions | When you need higher availability and have expert ops
| ZooKeeper ephemeral nodes | Strong consistency, watchable events | More operational complexity, higher latency | Leader election, complex coordination
| Database-based locks (SELECT FOR UPDATE, advisory locks) | No extra system if DB already central | DB load increases; not ideal cross-region | Low-frequency locks or when DB is already the arbiter

---

## BEFORE / AFTER: fixing a cache stampede

| Scenario | Before (no lock) | After (distributed lock) |
|---|---|---|
| Many concurrent requests for stale cache key | N requests all recompute the heavy value (CPU spike) | One request recomputes; others wait or serve slightly stale value (smoothed load) |
| Latency under load | High spikes, many timeouts | Smoother latency curve |
| Risk | Thundering herd | Reduced IO and CPU waste |

---

## Practical recipes and code

### 1) Redis single-instance lock (pattern)
- Use SET key value NX PX ttl
- Store a unique token (UUID) as the value
- When releasing, only delete if token matches (atomic check-and-delete via Lua)

Example (Python + redis-py):

```python
import uuid
from redis import Redis
r = Redis()

lock_key = 'lock:rebuild:user:123'
token = str(uuid.uuid4())
# acquire
acquired = r.set(lock_key, token, nx=True, px=5000)  # 5s lease
if acquired:
    try:
        do_heavy_work()
    finally:
        # safe release via Lua to avoid deleting someone else's lock
        lua = """
        if redis.call('get', KEYS[1]) == ARGV[1] then
            return redis.call('del', KEYS[1])
        else
            return 0
        end
        """
        r.eval(lua, 1, lock_key, token)
else:
    serve_stale_or_retry()
```

### 2) Why TTL / lease matters
If a process dies while holding a lock, the TTL lets the lock expire so others can proceed. But pick TTL > expected critical section time and be wary of long GC pauses or network stalls.

### 3) Using ZooKeeper ephemeral nodes (sketch)
- Create an ephemeral sequential node under /locks/resource/
- The holder is the node with the lowest sequence number
- Watch the previous node for deletion to get notified when you can become owner

This leverages ZooKeeper's consensus to ensure strong correctness.

---

## Common pitfalls (and how to avoid them)

- *Clock drift & lease extension*: Relying on system clocks to determine expiry can be fatal. Use TTLs managed by the lock store (Redis) rather than local clock checks. If you need to extend long-running work, implement a renewal background thread cautiously.

- *Wrong unlock*: Deleting a lock without verifying the token can remove someone else's lock after a TTL expiry + re-acquire sequence. Always check the token (use atomic Lua script on Redis).

- *Long critical sections*: Locks with long durations increase contention and failure blast radius. Break work into idempotent smaller steps where possible.

- *Using single Redis master as authoritative lock store*: It's simple and fast but introduces a single point of failure. Evaluate operational trade-offs or use consensus-backed systems for stronger guarantees.

- *Assuming locks provide liveness under partitions*: Under network partitions you can get split-brain where two clients think they hold the lock if the lock system is not strongly consistent.

- *Overusing locks*: Locks are coordination points — they serialize work. Prefer lockless designs (idempotency, optimistic concurrency, sharding) when possible.

---

## When to use a distributed lock

- Coordinate cache rebuilds (avoid stampede)
- Leader election for background jobs
- Serializing writes to an external system that can't accept concurrent changes
- Short critical sections where the overhead of a lock is small compared to the guarded work

When NOT to use: high-throughput paths that will become bottlenecks, or when idempotency/compensation can remove the need for strict mutual exclusion.

---

## Quick decision checklist

1. Is the work short and non-blocking? Yes → locks can be OK.
2. Can you design idempotent operations instead? Yes → prefer lockless.
3. Do you need strong safety under partitions? Yes → use ZooKeeper/consensus-based solution.
4. Does your ops team want to run and maintain another system? Consider DB-based locks as temporary fix.

---

## References & strategy
- Use token-based locks with TTL and atomic release.
- Prefer ephemeral nodes / consensus for strong correctness (at the cost of latency/complexity).
- Avoid long-held locks; make work idempotent, break into smaller steps.
keyTakeaways: Always use a unique token + TTL and an atomic check-before-delete when implementing locks (avoid plain DEL).
Choose the backing store by failure/safety needs: Redis for low-latency, ZooKeeper/consensus for strong guarantees.
Prefer lockless/idempotent designs when possible; locks serialize and can become bottlenecks.
